'''Mary Ellen Weber''' (born August 24, 1962) is an American executive, scientist, aviator, and a former [[NASA]] [[astronaut]].

== Education ==
Weber was born in [[Cleveland, Ohio]], and raised in [[Bedford Heights, Ohio]]. She graduated from [[Bedford High School (Ohio)|Bedford High School]] in 1980; received a [[Bachelor of Science]] in chemical engineering (with honors) from [[Purdue University]] in 1984,<ref name="nasabio">{{cite web |author1=Lyndon B. Johnson Space Center |author1-link=Johnson Space Center |title=Mary Ellen Weber |url=https://www.nasa.gov/sites/default/files/atoms/files/weber_mary.pdf |website=Biographical Data |publisher=[[NASA]] |access-date=April 28, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210428155638/https://www.nasa.gov/sites/default/files/atoms/files/weber_mary.pdf |archive-date=April 28, 2021 |location=[[Houston, Texas]] |date=March 2018 |url-status=live}}</ref> where she was a member of [[Phi Mu]] sorority;<ref name="phimus">{{cite web |author1=Phi Mu Fraternity |author1-link=Phi Mu |title=Famous Phi Mus Live The Creed, Too |url=https://phimublog.com/2016/03/04/famous-phi-mus-live-the-creed-too/ |website=A Vibrant View |access-date=April 28, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210428160049/https://phimublog.com/2016/03/04/famous-phi-mus-live-the-creed-too/ |archive-date=April 28, 2021 |date=March 4, 2016 |url-status=usurped}}</ref> received a [[Doctor of Philosophy|Ph.D.]] in physical chemistry from the [[University of California, Berkeley]] in 1988;<ref name="itapbio" /> and received an [[Master of Business Administration]] from [[Southern Methodist University]] in 2002.<ref name="itapbio">{{cite web |title=Mary Ellen Weber |url=https://www.rcac.purdue.edu/compute/weber/bio/ |website=ITaP Research Computing |publisher=[[Purdue University]] |access-date=April 28, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210428160408/https://www.rcac.purdue.edu/compute/weber/bio/ |archive-date=April 28, 2021 |url-status=live}}</ref>

== Pre-NASA career ==
As an undergrad, Weber was a chemical engineering intern at [[Ohio Edison]], [[Delco Electronics]], and [[3M]].<ref name="purdue-cradle">{{cite web |title=Cradle of Astronauts |url=https://engineering.purdue.edu/AAE/people/alumni/distinguished/Astronautbios |website=School of Aeronautics and Astronautics |publisher=[[Purdue University]] |access-date=April 28, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210428172236/https://engineering.purdue.edu/AAE/people/alumni/distinguished/Astronautbios |archive-date=April 28, 2021 |url-status=live}}</ref> In her doctoral research at Berkeley, she explored the physics of chemical reactions involving silicon.<ref name="chemaward">{{cite web |title=Dr. Mary Ellen Weber (BSChE'84) and Dr. Henry Sampson (BSChE'56) Receive Outstanding Chemical Engineer Award |url=https://engineering.purdue.edu/ChE/news/2009/DrMaryEllenWeberBSChE821784andDrHenrySampsonBSChE82 |website=Davidson School of Chemical Engineering |publisher=[[Purdue University]] |access-date=April 28, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210428172841/https://engineering.purdue.edu/ChE/news/2009/DrMaryEllenWeberBSChE821784andDrHenrySampsonBSChE82 |archive-date=April 28, 2021 |date=2009 |url-status=live}}</ref> At [[Texas Instruments]] she researched new processes and revolutionary equipment for making computer chips, with [[SEMATECH]] and [[Applied Materials]]. She holds one patent<ref name="patent">{{cite web |title=5,174,825: Uniform gas distributor to a wafer |url=https://pdfpiw.uspto.gov/25/748/051/1.pdf |publisher=[[United States Patent and Trademark Office]] |access-date=April 28, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210428174040/https://pdfpiw.uspto.gov/25/748/051/1.pdf |archive-date=April 28, 2021 |date=December 29, 1992 |url-status=live}}</ref> and published nine papers in scientific journals.

== NASA career ==
Weber was selected by NASA in the fourteenth group of astronauts in 1992.<ref name="92-42">{{cite web |last1=Hess |first1=Mark |last2=Schwartz |first2=Barbara |title=92-42: 1992 NASA Astronaut Candidates Selected |url=https://www.nasa.gov/home/hqnews/1992/92-042.txt |website=NASA News |publisher=[[NASA]] |access-date=April 28, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210428174719/https://www.nasa.gov/home/hqnews/1992/92-042.txt |archive-date=April 28, 2021 |format=TXT |date=March 31, 1992 |url-status=live}}</ref> During her ten-year career with NASA, she held several positions. She worked extensively in technology commercialization, and as part of a team reporting to NASA's chief executive, she worked directly with a venture capital firm to successfully identify and develop a business venture leveraging a space technology. In addition, Weber was the Legislative Affairs liaison at NASA Headquarters in [[Washington, D.C.]],<ref name="lookingsymp">{{cite web |last1=Garber |first1=Stephen J. |last2=Launius |first2=Roger |title=Looking Backward, Looking Forward: Forty Years of US Human Spaceflight Symposium |url=https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20030004255/downloads/20030004255.pdf |website=NTRS – NASA Technical Reports Server |publisher=[[NASA]] |access-date=April 28, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210428175453/https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20030004255/downloads/20030004255.pdf |archive-date=April 28, 2021 |location=[[Washington, DC]] |pages=231–232 |date=May 8, 2001 |url-status=live}}</ref> interfacing with Congress and traveling with NASA's chief executive. Prior to this appointment, she was chairman of the procurement board for the Biotechnology Program contractor,<ref name="texas-state-hr1113">{{cite web |title=Resolution – H. R. No. 1113 |url=https://capitol.texas.gov/tlodocs/81R/billtext/pdf/HR01113F.pdf |website=Texas Legislature Online |access-date=April 28, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210428175453/https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20030004255/downloads/20030004255.pdf |archive-date=April 28, 2021 |date=April 2, 2009 |url-status=live}}</ref> and she also served on a team that revamped the $2 billion plan for Space Station research facilities. Weber's principal technical assignments within the Astronaut Office included Shuttle launch preparations at the [[Kennedy Space Center]], payload and science development, and development of standards and methods for crew science training. A veteran of two space flights, [[STS-70]] and [[STS-101]], she was among the youngest to fly in space and she logged over 450 hours. She is the recipient of the [[NASA Exceptional Service Medal]]. She resigned from NASA in December 2002.<ref name="nasabio" />

=== Spaceflight experience ===
==== STS-70 ====
[[File:STS070-335-006 - Weber floats in the middeck in a yoga position (Retouched).jpg|thumb|right|Weber floats in a yoga position during STS-70]]
Weber was mission specialist 3 on the crew of [[STS-70]].<ref name="sts-summary">{{cite web |last1=Legler |first1=Robert D. |last2=Bennett |first2=Floyd V. |title=Space Shuttle Missions Summary |url=https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20110001406/downloads/20110001406.pdf |website=NTRS – NASA Technical Reports Server |publisher=[[NASA]] |access-date=April 27, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210427114154/https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20110001406/downloads/20110001406.pdf |archive-date=April 27, 2021 |location=Houston, Texas |date=September 2011 |url-status=live}}</ref>{{rp|103}}
[[Space Shuttle Discovery|Discovery]] launched from [[Kennedy Space Center Launch Complex 39B]] July 13, 1995, 13:41:55.078 UTC, STS-70 successfully delivered to orbit a critical $200 million NASA communications satellite, TDRS-G<ref name="ssmr-sts70">{{cite web |last1=Fricke |first1=Robert W. |title=STS-70: Space Shuttle Mission Report |url=https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19960020527/downloads/19960020527.pdf |website=NTRS – NASA Technical Reports Server |publisher=[[NASA]] |access-date=April 28, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210428182730/https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19960020527/downloads/19960020527.pdf |archive-date=April 28, 2021 |date=September 1995 |url-status=live}}</ref> to its 22-thousand-mile orbit above the equator. Weber deployed the satellite and also performed pioneering biotechnology experiments, growing colon cancer tissues never before possible to later become a leading NASA biotechnology spokesperson in this field. She was the prime spacewalk crewmember in the event a malfunction required a spacewalk, crew medical officer, and flight deck crew member for landing. STS-70 was known for its "All-Ohio crew"<ref name="funohiofacts">{{cite web |last1=Zona |first1=Kathleen |title=Fun Ohio Facts |url=https://www.nasa.gov/centers/glenn/about/bios/ohio_astronauts_fun_facts.html |website=Glenn Research Center |publisher=[[NASA]] |access-date=April 28, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210428184239/https://www.nasa.gov/centers/glenn/about/bios/ohio_astronauts_fun_facts.html |archive-date=April 28, 2021 |date=July 21, 2008 |url-status=live}}</ref> and for its last-minute launch delay due to woodpeckers,<ref name="woodpecker-ksc">{{cite web |last1=Dumoulin |first1=Jim |title=Woodpeckers damage STS-70 External Tank |url=https://science.ksc.nasa.gov/shuttle/missions/sts-70/woodpecker.html |website=[[Kennedy Space Center]] |publisher=[[NASA]] |access-date=April 28, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210428183114/https://science.ksc.nasa.gov/shuttle/missions/sts-70/woodpecker.html |archive-date=April 28, 2021 |date=June 2, 1995 |url-status=live}}</ref> becoming the "Woodpecker flight." The STS-70 mission was completed with a successful landing at the [[Shuttle Landing Facility]] July 22, 1995, 12:02 UTC after 142 orbits of the Earth, after traveling 3.7 million miles in 214 hours and 20 minutes.<ref name="ssmr-sts70" />

==== STS-101 ====
[[File:STS101-392-015 - STS-101 crew on aft flight deck during docking (Retouched).jpg|thumb|right|Weber (left) and her crewmates during STS-101 docking]]
Weber was mission specialist 1 on the crew of [[STS-101]].<ref name="sts-summary" />{{rp|141–142}}
[[Space Shuttle Atlantis|Atlantis]] launched from [[Kennedy Space Center Launch Complex 39B]] May 19, 2000, 10:11 UTC. STS-101 was the third Shuttle mission devoted to [[International Space Station]] construction—a critical mission, with no mission to the fledgling Station in over a year and batteries failing. The crew repaired and installed electrical and life-support components, both inside and out, and boosted the Station to a safe orbit. Weber was a flight deck crew member for launch, landing and Station rendezvous, drove Atlantis' 60-foot robotic arm to maneuver spacewalk crewmembers along the Station surface, and directed the logistics and transfer of over three thousand pounds of equipment. She also developed new crew checklists for engine failures during ascent and new procedures for robotic arm operations. The STS-101 mission—the subject of an A&E documentary, Mission Possible<ref name="WomenSpacefarers">{{cite book |last1=Cavallaro |first1=Umberto |title=Women Spacefarers: Sixty Different Paths to Space |date=2017 |publisher=Springer International Publishing |location=Milan |isbn=978-3-319-34047-0 |chapter=Mary E. Weber: From Skydiving to Stellar Strategies}}</ref>{{rp|201}}—was completed with successful landing at the Shuttle Landing Facility May 29, 2000, 06:20 UTC after 155 orbits of the Earth, after traveling 4.1 million miles in 236 hours and 9 minutes.<ref name="sts101summary">{{cite web |last1=Ryba |first1=Jeanne |title=STS-101 |url=https://www.nasa.gov/mission_pages/shuttle/shuttlemissions/archives/sts-101.html |website=Mission Archives |access-date=April 28, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210428185033/https://www.nasa.gov/mission_pages/shuttle/shuttlemissions/archives/sts-101.html |archive-date=April 28, 2021 |date=February 15, 2010 |url-status=live}}</ref>

== Post-NASA career ==
Weber is currently with Stellar Strategies, LLC,<ref name="Stellar">{{cite web |title=About |url=http://www.maryellenweber.com/about.html |website=Stellar Strategies |access-date=April 28, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210428201853/http://www.maryellenweber.com/about.html |archive-date=April 28, 2021 |url-status=live}}</ref> providing consulting services in strategies for operations in high-stakes business ventures, technology communications, and legislative strategy.<ref name="itapbio" /> She is also a speaker,<ref name="AstronautInsights">{{cite web |title=Mary Ellen Weber |url=http://www.astronautinsights.com/ |website=Astronaut Insights |access-date=April 28, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210428202246/https://www.astronautinsights.com/ |archive-date=April 28, 2021 |url-status=live}}</ref> with over twenty years of experience with a wide range of audiences and venues.

Prior to STELLAR Strategies, Weber was vice president for Government Affairs and Policy for nine years at the [[University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center]] in [[Dallas, Texas]].<ref name="WomenSpacefarers" />{{rp|202}}

== Personal life ==
Weber is married to Jerome Elkind, who is originally from [[Bayonne, New Jersey]].<ref name="nasabio" />

Having logged nearly 6,000 skydives,<ref name="Stellar" /> Weber is an active skydiver, with 13 silver and bronze medals to date at the U.S. National Skydiving Championships and a world record in 2002 for the largest freefall formation with 300 skydivers.<ref name="chemaward" /> In addition, she is an instrument-rated pilot, a skier, and a scuba diver.<ref name="nasabio" />
